children: By Patrick Thomas and Lindsay Wise
BOONE, Iowa-With just over a month to go until midterm elections, Republicans are facing the worst political environment in farm country in decades.

Tariffs and high prices for diesel, gas and fertilizer because of the war in Iran, along with President Trump's plans to import more beef, have soured the moods of America's farmers and ranchers, giving an opening for Democrats in what are typically solid red states.
Trump's trade war with China halted soybean exports, depressing prices for last year's crop and costing farmers billions of dollars. Tariffs have also made farm equipment more expensive.

"We need to get some other voices in there to push back a little bit on this stuff," said Nancy Danner, who farms thousands of acres of corn and soybeans with her husband, Kevin, in western Iowa. "We need as many changes as we can get."

Danner, a former independent who said she is voting for all Democrats this midterm cycle, blames Republicans for not pushing back on the war in Iran. She is frustrated with Trump's tariffs and said higher diesel fuel prices because of the war are hurting farmer profits, despite a recent uptick in grain prices.

Farmers have been a loyal voting bloc for Trump and the Republican Party for years. Many still support the president, especially on social issues, such as ending diversity initiatives, and say their short-term pain is needed for long-term changes to unfair trade policies with China. They are also skeptical of Democrats as a viable alternative.
But anxiety has been building over the past year, and Trump's favorability ratings have now dropped near record lows.
"If we're going to try to win back voters in the rural parts of America, this is as good a chance as we'll ever have," said Sen. John Hickenlooper (D., Colo.).

Republicans hold narrow majorities in the House and Senate, and their troubles in farm states are boosting Democrats' prospects for flipping both chambers and taking back governor mansions. Races in agricultural states such as Iowa-which went for Trump by 13 percentage points in 2024-are increasingly competitive for Democrats, who are bashing Trump's farm policies while calling for breaking up large agriculture companies.

In Iowa's governor race, farmer disaffection is boosting Rob Sand, the state auditor and the only Democrat currently elected to statewide office in Iowa. Recent polls show Sand leading Republican Zach Lahn, a businessman and farmer. The Iowa Farm Bureau Political Action Committee didn't endorse either candidate, the first time it sat out endorsing the race for governor since 2010. The group has endorsed all Republicans in recent election cycles.

Democrats believe they have a shot to flip three of Iowa's four House seats. There is also a hotly contested race for Iowa's open Senate seat between Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, a former TV news anchor, and Josh Turek, a state representative and Paralympic gold medalist in basketball.
'Close to a perfect storm'

Dave Wasserman, a senior elections analyst for the Cook Political Report, compared this election cycle to midterms in 1986, during an economic crisis that sent many farms and ranches into foreclosure, and 2006, an election seen as a referendum on the unpopular Iraq war and high fuel prices. Democrats flipped the Senate from red to blue in 1986 and increased their House majority. In 2006, they seized control of both chambers of Congress.
"Everything's got to go right for Democrats to win in these double-digit Trump states, but this is close to a perfect storm for Democrats," Wasserman said.

Michael Sersland, an Iowa farmer with about 1,100 acres, is still undecided on the midterm races and is waiting until Election Day to make up his mind. Farmers are Republicans, he said, but they aren't fans of the war and rising costs.
"I'll make a final decision that day," he said.

Sen. Joni Ernst (R., Iowa), who is retiring after this term, said high diesel prices-now above $6.50 a gallon-are weighing on farmers. "I would say it's rough now. If we can stabilize those fuel prices, it does become better for our farmers. But it's still rough," she said.

Outside of Iowa, ranchers in states such including Nebraska, Kansas and Texas, are fuming over Trump's recent plan to import 300,000 metric tons-or roughly 660 million pounds-of beef from South America free of tariffs. The move, aimed at lowering high consumer prices, infuriated ranchers. The National Cattlemen's Beef Association, the largest trade group for cattle ranchers, with more than 25,000 members, said government intervention will hurt ranchers and prevent long-term stability in the beef industry.

Dan Osborn, an independent running against Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts in Nebraska-where cattle outnumber people three to one-recently ran an advertisement criticizing Republicans for supporting policies that would bring in more beef from South America.
ICE raids hit beef production

Cattlemen groups from Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas spoke out against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent activity in southwest Kansas this past week. The area is home to several massive beef processing plants and large feedlots-where cattle are fattened before slaughter. ICE's presence delayed shifts and hampered beef production at some facilities after some employees didn't show up for work.
The operations are "?having a massive chilling effect on the legal, documented, skilled workers," the groups said, adding that the ?disruptions will lead to higher beef prices.
While cattlemen are angry with the Trump administration, Democrats still have a long way to go to win the trust of rural ranchers.

"Politics has been frustrating," said northeast Iowa rancher Wayne Vorwald at a farm trade show in the state this month. "There are plenty of angry cattlemen around here." Nonetheless, Vorwald says that he can't bring himself to vote for a Democrat.

Quentin Dailey, a Lexington, Neb., cattle rancher, said his main fear is that if Democrats regain control of the Senate, Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey, a vegan, will take over as chair of the Senate Agriculture Committee.
"That does not bode well for our industry," he said.

In the cattle-heavy 15th congressional district in Texas, Democrat Bobby Pulido is running against incumbent Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz. Cook Political Report moved the race from "lean Republican" to "tossup" this week, even though Trump won the district by 18 percentage points in 2024. Pulido said he's heard anecdotally that farmers and ranchers are staying home this election cycle. He hopes to win them over.
"I have friends that are cattle ranchers themselves, and actually they voted for Trump, and they're really angry," Pulido said.
